<document_content>
# tides

A tiny project for trying pulp. It mixes code, notes, data, and a notebook,
so you can see how each kind of file lands in one dump.

- `src/` is a small Rust crate that finds the high tide in a day of readings.
- `proofs/` holds a Lean lemma.
- `data/` has the readings as CSV and the gauge settings as JSON.
- `notebooks/` explores the readings; its output cell is kept only when
  notebook outputs are on.
- `docs/` has a PDF and a Word file, extracted to text.
- `site/` is the one-page HTML description.
- `Cargo.lock` starts unticked: lockfiles rarely help a model.
- `data/archive.zip` starts unticked: turn on archives to unpack it.

//! Parse tide readings and find the extremes.

/// One sea-level reading from a tide gauge.
#[derive(Debug, Clone, PartialEq)]
pub struct Reading {
    pub time: String,
    pub height_m: f64,
}

impl Reading {
    /// Parse `time,height_m` from one CSV line.
    pub fn parse(line: &str) -> Option<Self> {
        let (time, height) = line.split_once(',')?;
        Some(Self {
            time: time.trim().to_string(),
            height_m: height.trim().parse().ok()?,
        })
    }
}

/// The reading with the greatest height, if any.
pub fn highest(readings: &[Reading]) -> Option<&Reading> {
    readings.iter().max_by(|a, b| a.height_m.total_cmp(&b.height_m))
}

<source>src/main.rs</source>
<document_content>
use tides::{Reading, highest};

fn main() {
    let csv = include_str!("../data/readings.csv");
    let readings: Vec<Reading> = csv.lines().skip(1).filter_map(Reading::parse).collect();
    match highest(&readings) {
        Some(r) => println!("high tide: {:.2} m at {}", r.height_m, r.time),
        None => println!("no readings"),
    }
}
